text: Smallholder farmers in Preah Vihear commonly receive low prices for rice, cashew, and other crops for structural reasons that are worth explaining to a farmer asking 'why is my price so low,' not just how to sell. During peak harvest windows -- the main wet-season rice harvest and the dry-season cashew harvest -- large numbers of smallholders sell at the same time, creating a supply glut that pushes prices down regardless of quality. Farmers also typically lack access to real-time regional wholesale price information, creating an information gap between them and traders who move between many villages and know current prices across a wider area -- this asymmetry weakens a farmer's negotiating position. Limited on-farm storage and drying capacity adds pressure to sell quickly rather than wait for better prices, and farmers who took on debt for seasonal inputs (seed, fertilizer) often face urgent cash needs right at harvest, exactly when prices are weakest. Poor rural road access during the wet season further restricts a farmer's ability to reach alternative buyers, which can concentrate bargaining power in the hands of whichever trader is willing to travel that route. None of this means selling to a local trader is a bad choice -- traders provide a real service (transport, aggregation, immediate payment) -- but understanding these structural pressures helps a farmer make a more informed choice rather than assuming a low price simply reflects their crop's quality. Practical, low-cost steps that can modestly improve a farmer's position: basic on-farm sorting and cleaning before sale (separating out foreign material, moisture-damaged, or visibly poor-quality product) to present a more consistent batch; comparing prices from more than one buyer when time allows, including by phone where mobile signal and informal price-sharing networks exist; avoiding an immediate distress sale at the very peak of the harvest glut where storage and cash flow allow; and coordinating with other farmers or a local group to combine volume and negotiate together, since traders often pay more per unit for a larger, aggregated quantity than for many small individual lots. Do not assume a specific current price, buyer, or transport cost -- these vary by village, season, and year and should be confirmed locally rather than treated as fixed facts.
